messages.body_plain:
Distance Sampling Training Workshops 2019

In August 2019, the Centre for Research into Ecological and
Environmental Modelling (CREEM) at the University of St Andrews,
Scotland, is hosting a series of linked, training workshops on distance
sampling survey methods and analysis.

Introduction to R (for distance sampling): 19-20 August 2019

Many of the options available in the Distance for Windows program
(Thomas et al. 2013) are now available in R (R Core Team, 2018)
packages. The goal of this two-day workshop is to introduce participants
to the R language and software for statistics, in the context of
analysis of distance sampling data.

Introduction to Distance Sampling (using R): 21-23 August 2019

This workshop will give participants a solid grounding in the basic
methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys. The
statistical programming language R will be used for all computer
sessions and therefore the workshop will be invaluable for those wishing
to make the switch from the Distance for Windows program to R.

Advanced-level Distance Sampling: 26-30 August 2019

This workshop will cover simulation of distance sampling surveys for
design purposes, survey and analysis methods for dealing with imperfect
detection on the trackline (double-observer methods) and spatial
modelling of distance sampling data (as described in Miller et al.
(2013)). The statistical programming language R will be used for all
computer sessions.

For more information see the
https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-workshops-st-andrews-2019/
or contact Louise Burt (l...@st-andrews.ac.uk).

References

Miller DL, Rexstad E, Thomas L, Marshall L, Laake J (2019)  Distance
Sampling in R. Journal of Statistical Software, forthcoming
https://doi.org/10.1101/063891

Miller DL, Burt ML, Rexstad EA & Thomas L (2013) Spatial models for
distance sampling data: recent developments and future directions.
Methods in Ecology and Evolution 4 (11):1001–1010.
https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12105.

R Core Team (2018) R: A language and environment for statistical
computing. R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria. URL
https://www.R-project.org/

Thomas L, Buckland ST, Rexstad EA, Laake JL, Strindberg S, Hedley SL,
Bishop JRB, Marques TA & Burnham KP (2010)  Distance software: design
and analysis of distance sampling surveys for estimating population
size. Journal of Applied Ecology 47: 5-14.  DOI:
10.1111/j.1365-2664.2009.01737.x

messages.subject: Documentation confusion for predict.dsm() and possible bug
messages.subject_clean: Documentation confusion for predict.dsm() and possible bug
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm working on a DSM where the response is "density". While experimenting with predict(), I discovered that it does not return what it used to (before Issue #33 was fixed), and what I (perhaps naively) expected.

Also, I think there's a bug when off.set is not supplied to predict.dsm() (more on that below).

I'm posting here so that other poor naive souls might avoid the same mistake.

Here's a minimal example using code adapted from Len Thomas' posting of Issue 33 here: https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/dsm/issues/33 where it was realized that the off.set was not being taken into account in models with "density" as the response.

library(Distance)
library(dsm)

# load the Gulf of Mexico dolphin data (see ?mexdolphins)
data(mexdolphins)

# fit a detection function and look at the summary
hr.model <- ds(distdata, max(distdata$distance),
               key = "hr", adjustment = NULL)
summary(hr.model)

# fit a simple smooth of x and y to estimated density
mod1 <- dsm(density~s(x,y), hr.model, segdata, obsdata, family=gaussian())
summary(mod1)
# predict over a grid
mod1.pred <- predict(mod1, preddata, preddata$area)
# calculate the predicted ***abundance*** over the grid. Naively reading the manual I did not expect this to return abundance,
sum(mod1.pred)
#24777.49

The crux of the matter is that after reading the manual for predict.dsm() I unthinkingly expected it to return density in the same units as the data passed to predict.gam() (ie. without multiplying by the off.set) like it used to. However, after looking at the code for predict.dsm(), reading the discussion about Issue #33 at the link above, and the helpful posts from Eric Rexstad here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/predict.dsm%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/kKp8QG5k3eo/1pYcUpcrpD0J I realized that this isn't that is no longer the case.

Predict.dsm() now multiplies the predictions returned by predict.gam() by off.set, for models where the response is "density" (or one of it's synonyms) . From reading the manual for predict.dsm() I did not realize this. Probably because the last time I used predict() it was before Issue #33 was fixed. I know, I know.... at this point you're thinking "Well, what did you think it was going to do with the off.set??". I guess I just naively looked at the output from predict() prior to the Issue #33 fix and didn't think too much more about it.

Thus if you just want density in the same units as in the gam you just need to do:

mod1.pred <- predict(mod1, preddate, 1)

 I'd suggest modifying the documentation for off.set in predict.dsm() to mention this explicitly:

off.set

area of each of the cells in the prediction grid. Should be in the same units as the segments/distances given to dsm. This will be multiplied by the predictions from the gam. Ignored if there is already a column in newdata called off.set.

And perhaps change the Value section to read:

> predicted values on the response scale (density/abundance depending on the value of off.set).

I'll volunteer to do this and add an example (based on the code above) showing what happens for different values of off.set if there's interest from the dsm gods. Or perhaps I should offer to expand the vignette?

Now for the possible bug:

The manual implicitly indicates (and Eric's post here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/predict.dsm%7Csort:date/distance-sampling/kKp8QG5k3eo/1pYcUpcrpD0J explicitly states) that leaving the off.set out of the call to predict() will accomplish the same thing as:

mod1.pred <- predict(mod1, preddate, 1)

However, when I do:

mod1.pred <- predict(mod1, preddate)
sum(mod1.pred)
# 0!

it always returns 0 (because off.set is NULL by default and multiplying anything by NULL is 0.

I'd suggest the following code from the end of predict.dsm()

 # actually do the predict call
  result <- predict(object, newdata, type=type, ...)

  ## if we have density do the predictions on response scale right
  # grab standard error
  se.fit <- list(...)$se.fit
  if((c(object$formula[[2]]) %in% c("D", "density", "Dhat", "density.est"))){
    # only need do this for type="response" but need to make sure
    # that the standard errors are okay too
    if(type=="response" & (is.null(se.fit) || !se.fit)){
      result <- result*off.set
    }else if(type=="response" & se.fit){
      result$fit <- result$fit*off.set
      result$se.fit <- result$se.fit*off.set
    }
  }

Be changed to:

 # actually do the predict call
  result <- predict(object, newdata, type=type, ...)

  ## if we have density do the predictions on response scale right
  # grab standard error
  se.fit <- list(...)$se.fit
  if((c(object$formula[[2]]) %in% c("D", "density", "Dhat", "density.est"))){

    # make sure off.set has a value before multiplying
    if (is.null(off.set))
      off.set <- 1

    # only need do this for type="response" but need to make sure
    # that the standard errors are okay too
    if(type=="response" & (is.null(se.fit) || !se.fit)){
      result <- result*off.set
    }else if(type=="response" & se.fit){
      result$fit <- result$fit*off.set
      result$se.fit <- result$se.fit*off.set
    }
  }

I can open an issue on GitHub if that's helpful.

Thanks!
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave, hi listfolk,

Thanks for the thorough bug report and suggestion!

I've added a bit of extra text to the "Value" section of the
documentation, along the lines of what you suggest. (I didn't add your
suggestion for off.set, as I can't put together a wording that's both
simple and technically correct...) The wording is at
https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/dsm/blob/bf7a4d7eaf6ffa02274a5c46bb02f0b5e952aa79/R/predict.dsm.R#L13

Thanks also for catching the bug in off.set=NULL. I've made some changes
to the code that fix this. If you can run your code and check you get
what you expect that would be ace.

Changes will be in the next CRAN release of dsm. In the meantime the
development version of dsm can be obtained using
devtools::install_github("DistanceDevelopment/dsm")

cheers,
--dave

I have a question about effort calculation when it’s used with camera traps as a point transect

I have to calculate the effort for a project using 21 traps for 15 days in each point active for 24 h per day, i have set up the traps for 20 seconds video with a delay of 2 sec. The detection angle 0.733RAD.

What is confusing me is if I have to calculate the effort for 24 h at each point or only the time when I shot the video of my target species

Any suggestion for the calculation?

Thank for any clarification

Best

Emiliano

messages.body_plain:
Emiliano

I assume you are making use of the methods described in the paper

Howe, Eric J., Stephen T. Buckland, Marie-Lyne Després‐Einspenner, and Hjalmar S. Kühl. 2017. Distance Sampling with Camera Traps. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 8 (11): 1558–65.  https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12790.

The authors of that paper have provided their data in a repository described at the end of the paper:

"The data files from which densities of Maxwell’s duikers were estimated using Distance software, and data describing start times of videos  of Maxwell’s duikers, have been archived at the Dryad data repository (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad. b4c70) (Howe et al. 2017)."

If you visit that repository link, they provide their data, as well as a description of the data, where I think you will find your answer regarding how effort was calculated:

"Filmed Maxwell's duikers were assigned to distance intervals; recorded distances are the midpoints of the intervals. "Sample.Label" references the trap location. "Effort" is temporal effort, i.e. the number of 2-second time-steps over which the camera operated. "multiplier" describes spatial effort, as the proportion of a circle covered by the angle of view of the camera. The data is formatted as a "flatfile" suitable for use with distance sampling software including Distance and associated R packages."

I hope this is helpful.

Eric Rexstad

messages.subject: Re: Sample Effort with camera Traps
messages.subject_clean: Sample Effort with camera Traps
messages.body_plain:
Hello Emiliano,

I think of temporal sampling effort as the number of opportunities (in time) to record distances to animals. We defined temporal sampling effort at one CT location as the total duration of sampling at that location, divided by the length of the time step between the predetermined "snapshot moments" at which distances are recorded. So, if the CT operates for one hour (Tk = 3600 seconds), and we record distance at 2-second intervals (t = 2), then temporal effort is Tk / t = 3600 / 2.

The fact that CTs observe less than a complete circle can be included in your estimate of "Effort" at a location by dividing the horizontal angle of view of the camera in radians ("theta"), by a 2*pi (radians in a complete circle).  Combining Tk / 2 (temporal effort) and theta / 2*pi (spatial effort < a complete circle) yields the definition of effort presented in the article ( theta * Tk / 2*pi*t.)

Alternatively, you can use "Effort" (in Distance) to define temporal effort only, and use theta / 2*pi as a "multiplier". This is the approach we took with the duiker analysis.

All the best,
Eric

Thanks for asking your question to the Distance list.  I recommend you have a look at the lectures and exercises associated with distance sampling at our online workshop:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
Materials there will help with some of the basics.  But to your specific questions
distance and angle measurements in the field.  When using the R package, you'll need to covert those measurements to perpendicular distances from the transect. Here's a bit of code showing the perpendicular distance for an angular distance of 10 units, sweeping through the 360 degrees of the compass
distance <- 10  # meters lets say
for (bearing in seq(1,360,by=5)) {
  radian.bearing <- bearing * (pi/180)
  perdis <- abs(distance * sin(radian.bearing))
  cat(i, d.r, perdis, "\n")
}
multiple visits to a transect:  no universal solution to this, it depends upon what is biologically relevant.  However, it is seldom the case there are sufficient detections in a single day to produce reliable abundance estimates.  It is often the situation that data are pooled across days, then a single estimate is produced from the pooled data; that single estimate is an average of animal abundance in the study area across the visits.  Be sure to adjust the effort when pooling data across visits (effort = line length * number of visits).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Antonella, hi listfolk,

This is a good question and one that has a bit of a technical answer.

The models fitted by dsm are just GAMs, as fitted by mgcv. So, anything
that applies to mgcv models also applies to dsm. A (somewhat technical)
answer is in ?summary.gam, which describes (at least some of) the output
in the summary table for dsm too.

A quick explanation:

You set a maximum degrees of freedom (sometimes called complexity or
basis size) when you setup a smooth in your model. This is done using
the k=... parameter in s() or te(). The value is set automatically if
you don't supply it (see ?choose.k for more information on how to set
k). This parameter sets the absolute limit on how wiggly the model will be.

During model fitting, we don't use all of those degrees of freedom
(usually), as the penalty reduces the wigglyness to be the "right"
amount. This gives us the EDF, the effective degrees of freedom for that
term. This is how wiggly the model things that term should be.

If we want to do a significance test and ask "should we have this term
in the model?" (equivalently "should this term be 0?"), we need to have
some degrees of freedom for that test. So we could use k, above, to do
that. This is fine but often we set k too large because we don't know
how wiggly the true smooth is and we want to make sure that there is
enough flexibility in the smooth from the outset. If we use the k in
that case, we might end up with (non)significant effects when really it
was just because we set k to big. For that reason we set a reference
degrees of freedom to use for the tests (that gives us the p-values at
the end of each line).

The technical side of this is covered in this paper:
https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article-abstract/100/1/221/192816?redirectedFrom=fulltext

Short answer: ref.df is the degrees of freedom that will be used for the
tests to see if the smooths are significant.

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Suzi

Welcome to the distance sampling list.  I can't answer all of your questions from the figures you provide.  However, I make three observations:

a warning message from Distance does not necessarily mean the results are incorrect; warnings are generated by the software to indicate that something seems unusual and that you should investigate more closely.  Without looking at your project, I don't know the nature of the warning, but I'll speculate about that below
looking at your results table, the delta-AIC scores are small for all models, meaning there is little to choose between them.  However I see that you included the negative exponential model.  It is a model without a shoulder, meaning it falls away steeply at small distances from the transect.  We usually discourage use of that model, unless the biological situation warrants.  It seems surprising to me that in sampling trees, the detection function would fall off very rapidly; but you were the data collector--you must assess whether to include the negative exponential in your model set
finally looking at the data table you provide, it appears that you placed only a single transect in each of your habitat type strata, for which you wish to make a comparison.  With a single transect, encounter rate variance cannot be assessed (no variability with a sample of size 1).  I suspect that may be the nature of the warning message Distance has produced. Suzi

Thanks for sharing your data and field experiences.

It is a bit awkward that you exerted so little effort in the secondary forest.  With only 10 detections on a single transect, there is little you can say about fig density in this habitat.  A more sound survey design would have been to allocate sampling effort into each habitat type prior to beginning to collect data, rather than choosing when to stop data collection based upon the data.

Survey design aside, one way to analysed data from two habitats is to combine them in a single Distance project, as they were part of a single study as I have done below (perpendicular distances in observation layer not shown).

I then request a stratified analysis, and density estimates for each stratum using this screen:
This will produce density estimates for each stratum using the detection function fitted with detections from each stratum.  That is a challenge here because of the small number of detections in the secondary forest stratum; but having separate detection functions makes the two density estimates independent; which they would not be if a shared detection function was fitted to the data pooled across strata.

As an aside, note your data have a strong peak at distances <1m.  There is little information about the detection function from the small number of detections > 7m.  So perhaps some truncation should be used, depleting an already small number of detections.

messages.body_plain:
Good day,

I noticed that although the default estimator of the encounter rate variance among point transects in Program Distance is Fewster et al.'s (2009) varP2 (presented in web appendix B, equation 24), only their varP3 is available to estimate the encounter rate variance for point transects in the 'mrds' R package.

Is there a reason for this?

Our data arise from a camera trap distance sampling survey. The design was systematic (a grid). In spite of this, after reading Fewster et al.'s article and the Web Appendix, I was planning to use varP2 with our data, because the number of "visits" to each point varies, and it does not seem reasonable to assume that the encounter rate is similar throughout the region. Also, from the manual for Program Distance: "Fewster et al. (2009) found that R2 slightly out-performed R3 in simulations, and for this reason as well as because no assumptions are made about animal distribution, this estimator is the default in Distance.... For point transects, the equivalent estimator to R2 is P2."

Eric

messages.body_plain:
Anthony

Several answers to this question, ranging from simple (and perhaps incorrect) to more complex:

if you have species recorded at the observation level of your data, you could use Distance and simply ignore the species field.  This would pool data across species producing an abundance estimate.  However, such an analysis would assume detection probability does not differ between species.
You could employ the MCDS (multiple covariate distance sampling) engine and use species as a covariate in the detection function and ask for a global density estimate.  That would produce distinct detection functions for multiple species and the density/abundance estimates produced would take the differing detection functions into account.
A word of caution however.  I'm not sure how far you could extend the inference about year-to-year abundance differences when using information from a single transect.  I'm not certain what you meant by 'for a given transect.'

messages.body_plain:
Nick

You're off to a good start.  A few points
The reason you have the same estimate for two strata is because there are the same number of detections in both strata (14) and you are fitting a common detection function (same function for both strata).
I'm guessing this is just a portion of your data to get started.  Otherwise, it is an awkward study design with only a single transect in each stratum.  With that design, you have no measure of encounter rate variability in each stratum.  You're also low on the number of detections for making inference.,
The shape of your histograms look fairly good--a bit of heaping at small distances perhaps but both the half normal and hazard rate appear to fit adequately.
Are the perpendicular distances measured in meters or feet?  Either way, I'm a little surprised that you are able to detect pellet groups out to 12 (meters or feet).
Regarding the inclusion of defecation rates to convert pellet density to deer density; that is something that is not possible to do in the Distance R package just now.  It is an area of programming activity just now and we hope to have multipliers implemented by late this summer.  It is not very hard to do manually; the tricky bit comes it propagating the variability in defecation rates along with the uncertainty in pellet density properly.
You can read about including defecation rates (and uncertainty) to convert pellet density to animal density in our online workshop materials:   https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter6/

Eric Rexstad

There is individual body size (perhaps serving as a surrogate of species, under the assumption that detectability is a function of body size rather than behaviour).  There is group size (number of individuals in a detected cluster) that may influence detectability (under the assumption that larger groups are more easily detected than small groups at large distances).
